Johann Blankenfeld
yoh'hahn blahn'ken-felt
n. (c. 1471–1527; Archbishop of Riga, who fought the Reformation in Livonia and lost)
Blankenfeld, a German surname from blank, white or bright, and Feld, field; the white field.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Johann Blankenfeld came of a Berlin patrician family, took doctorates in both laws at Bologna, and rose through the Livonian church as Bishop of Reval, then of Dorpat, and from 1524 Archbishop of Riga, holding all three sees at once for a time. He spent his archiepiscopate trying to stop the Reformation: he pressed the Emperor and the Pope for mandates against the Riga preachers, worked to bring the Order and the towns into a Catholic front, and was suspected of inviting Moscow's help against his own city. The Order arrested him in 1525 at Ronneburg; he was released after renouncing his foreign dealings, set out for the Emperor to argue his case, and died at Torda in Transylvania in 1527. The archbishopric did not recover. The dictionary records him as the Baltic's instance of Gamaliel's warning being ignored: “But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God” (Act 5:39).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an archbishop as a chief bishop having jurisdiction over other bishops; to overthrow as to demolish, to subvert, to destroy; and vain as empty, worthless, having no substance or value.

expand to see more

ARCHBISHOP, n. A chief bishop; a church dignitary of the first class; a metropolitan bishop who superintends the conduct of other bishops.

OVERTHROW, v.t. To turn upside down; to demolish; to subvert; to destroy; to defeat.

VAIN, a. [L. vanus.] Empty; worthless; having no substance, value or importance; fruitless; ineffectual.

COUNSEL, n. Advice; deliberation; a plan or purpose formed; the design of God.

PLACE, n. A particular portion of space; station; office; rank; a dwelling.

Key Scripture

Act 5:39 — "But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God."

Pro 21:30 — "There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the LORD."

Mat 15:9 — "But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men."

Joh 11:48 — "If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him: and the Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation."

Modern Corruption

Archbishop of Riga from 1524 who held three Livonian sees, petitioned Emperor and Pope against the Reformation, was arrested by the Order in 1525, and died in 1527.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Honesty requires two admissions. Blankenfeld was not a fool or a monster: he was a trained canonist defending an office and an order he held to be of divine institution, in a province visibly falling apart, and some of his fears about what would follow were justified. And the dictionary should not pretend the charge against him of seeking Russian intervention against Riga is proven; it was alleged by his enemies and he denied it. What is certain is that he spent his whole archiepiscopate on external force — mandates, alliances, arrests — and never once on an answer to Knopken's exposition of Romans.

The principle to recover is that an institution cannot be defended against God by procedure. Gamaliel's caution is addressed to men with full legal authority over the preachers in front of them: “But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God” (Act 5:39). Proverbs puts the limit absolutely — “There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the LORD” (Pro 21:30). And the council in John shows what the calculation looks like from inside, when a man weighs his place and nation against the truth of what is happening: “If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him” (Joh 11:48).

Greek kataluo (G2647), to overthrow or dissolve; Hebrew 'etsah (H6098), counsel or purpose.

Usage

"“But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it” (Act 5:39) — mandates sought from Emperor and Pope against the Riga preachers."

"“There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the LORD” (Pro 21:30) — arrested by his own Order at Ronneburg, 1525."

"“If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him” (Joh 11:48) — died at Torda in 1527 on his way to the Emperor."
